sections.h2: How long before an occupant can claim the land?
sections.html:
Ten years. A Nebraska occupant gains nothing from time unless every element of adverse possession is met for that whole period. The period comes from 25-202, which sets a ten-year limit on actions to recover title or possession of land.

The Nebraska Supreme Court spelled out what the occupant must show in Rentschler v. Walnofer (1979): possession that is actual, continuous, exclusive and notorious, hostile to the record owner, and held under a claim of ownership, for the full ten years. The court added that the land must be used for a purpose it is suited for. The claimant carries the burden and must prove the case by a preponderance of the evidence.

There is no shorter clock for squatters. Moving into a vacant house for a few weeks gives no title. What a short-term intruder can do is create a possession problem the owner then has to resolve through the courts or the police.

Public land follows other rules. Section 25-202(1) says no limitation period runs against a county, city, town, village, school or other listed public body trying to recover roads, streets, alleys, public grounds and town lots.

Several common situations fail the test because the occupier never held the property against the owner's rights. Nebraska decisions draw these lines.

SituationHow Nebraska courts treat it
Living there with the owner's permissionPermissive possession cannot ripen into adverse possession until the change of position is brought home to the owner (Imperial Service Corp. v. Phipps, 1980)
A tenant who stays after the leaseA tenant cannot hold adversely until surrendering possession or giving the landlord unequivocal notice that the lease no longer governs (Kennedy v. Gottschalk, 1941)
A parent and child sharing a propertyPossession between parent and child is deemed permissive (Chase v. Lavelle, 1921)
A co-owner in possessionNotice of a claim to the entire estate must be brought home to the other co-owners plainly and unequivocally (Gramann v. Beatty, 1938)
A claim like a life estateNot a claim of ownership (Lewis v. Poduska, 1992)
An occupant who disclaims title earlyDisclaiming before the period runs bars the claim (Weisel v. Hobbs, 1940)

So a house that a relative or former renter has lingered in for years is not automatically lost. It also explains why owners should put permission in writing and react when a stay turns hostile.

Boundary disputes are where adverse possession is most likely to touch an ordinary homeowner. Several Nebraska decisions deal with fences.

  • In Ohme v. Thomas (1938), parties who treated a fence as the boundary for the full ten years, without interruption, gained title to land that had been wrongly enclosed.
  • In Conkey v. Anderson Farms (1980), the court reasoned the same way where a fence was built as a boundary even though it was not the true line.
  • Weiss v. Meyer (1981) held that adverse possession rests on the occupant's intent as shown by acts, and that the intent can be mistaken. A claimant who occupies up to the wrong line, believing it is the true one, can satisfy the test.

If a neighbor's garage, driveway or fence has sat over the line for a decade, that can surface in a survey or title review just as you try to close. A boundary fix or a recorded agreement is far easier to finish before an offer than during one.

sections.h2: Removing someone with no right to be there
sections.html:
The civil route is a forcible entry and detainer action, and it starts with a written notice to leave. 25-21,220 lists who can be sued this way. That includes tenants holding over and, in subsection (5), a settler or occupier of land without color of title when the complainant has the right of possession.

Before filing, 25-21,221 requires the owner to notify the adverse party to leave. The notice must be served at least three days before the action begins, by leaving a written copy with that person or at the usual place of abode. If the person cannot be found in the county, the notice may be left at or posted on the premises. The Court of Appeals called this three-day notice necessary to obtain an order of restitution in I. P. Homeowners v. Morrow (2003).

The remedy has limits. In Woodsonia Hwy 281 v. American Multi-Cinema (2025), the Nebraska Supreme Court held that a forcible entry and detainer case must be dismissed when the right to possession depends on resolving the defendant's own right in the property. A genuine title dispute belongs in a different action, such as one to quiet title, which is also subject to the ten-year statute under Olsen v. Olsen (2003).

sections.h2: When an unwanted occupant becomes a criminal trespasser
sections.html:
Entering or secretly remaining in a building while knowing you have no license or privilege to be there is first degree criminal trespass, a Class I misdemeanor under 28-520. Second degree criminal trespass covers other places where notice against trespass has been given.

Under 28-521, notice can be given three ways: by telling the person directly, by posting signs in a way likely to catch the intruder's attention, or by fencing or enclosing the land to exclude intruders. Second degree trespass is a Class III misdemeanor. It rises to a Class II misdemeanor if the person defies an order to leave that the owner or an authorized person gives personally.

Someone who walked in uninvited stands differently from a former tenant or family member who once had permission. For the second kind, a written notice to leave and a copy of your deed give you a record of the order the statute refers to.

The aim is to keep the ten-year clock from ever starting, and to leave a paper trail if someone tests it. A few habits follow from the rules above.

  • Inspect the property on a regular schedule and note the dates. The occupation must be actual, notorious and continuous to count against you.
  • Put any permission to stay in writing, including who may live there and until when.
  • Post notices and keep fences and locks in repair, which lines up with the notice methods in 28-521.
  • Serve the three-day written notice early if someone is staying without consent.
  • Record your own deed. Hadley v. Platte Valley Cattle Co. (1943) held that a fee simple holder under an unrecorded deed does not forfeit title by failing to assert it, but a recorded deed is easier for everyone to see.
  • Do not wait years. The death of the party against whom the statute is running does not stop it, so it continues against heirs (McNeill v. Schumaker, 1913).

That last point matters for inherited houses that sit empty while family members decide what to do.

sections.h2: Selling with an occupant or a possession dispute
sections.html:
An occupied house is harder to sell on the open market, because a buyer is charged with notice of the rights of anyone in actual possession. Grand Island Hotel Corp. v. Second Island Development Co. (1974), cited under 76-238, applies that rule to a tenant in actual possession.

So unresolved occupants and boundary claims tend to come up in the buyer's title review. We buy Nebraska houses as-is, including some with tenants, holdovers or messy ownership history, and we can talk through what a sale would look like. We are not lawyers, so if someone claims ownership of your property, speak with a Nebraska attorney first.

faqs.q: Do squatters have rights in Nebraska?
faqs.a: Only if they meet adverse possession for ten full years under 25-202 and the cases applying it. The occupant must show actual, continuous, exclusive, notorious and hostile possession under a claim of ownership. Time spent there with the owner's permission generally does not count.

faqs.q: How long is the adverse possession period in Nebraska?
faqs.a: Ten years. Section 25-202 limits actions to recover title or possession of land to ten years after the cause of action accrues, and Nebraska courts use the same period for adverse possession.

faqs.q: What notice do I give a squatter in Nebraska before filing for eviction?
faqs.a: A written notice to leave, served at least three days before the action begins under 25-21,221. It can be handed to the person, left at the usual place of abode, or posted at the premises if the person cannot be found in the county.

faqs.q: Is it a crime to stay in someone's house in Nebraska without permission?
faqs.a: It can be. Entering or secretly remaining in a building knowing you have no license or privilege to be there is first degree criminal trespass under 28-520, a Class I misdemeanor. Defying a personal order to leave other property raises second degree trespass to a Class II misdemeanor under 28-521.

faqs.q: Can a former tenant claim my Nebraska house by staying after the lease ends?
faqs.a: Not by simply staying. Under Kennedy v. Gottschalk, a tenant cannot hold adversely to the landlord until surrendering possession or giving unequivocal notice that the lease no longer governs. Holdover tenants can also be removed through forcible entry and detainer under 25-21,220.
